debates.minor-heading: Housing Supply and Affordability Bill 2012; Second Reading

speech.p: That this bill be now read a second time.

This bill is about one simple idea: every Australian deserves a secure and affordable place to call home. Too many families in my electorate are spending more than half of their income on rent, and too many young people have given up on ever saving a deposit for a first home.

The bill funds 20,000 new social housing dwellings over four years and requires states to report on housing supply targets. It also establishes a national rental affordability scheme so that tenants on low incomes can find homes close to work.
Housing affordability is not only a housing issue; it shapes where people can work and where children go to school. I commend the bill to the House.
It will push up rents and you know it!
On a point of order on relevance about the housing bill.
The minister told the House last week:
Every dollar we spend on social housing is a dollar saved in our hospitals.

That may be a good line, but the hospitals in my electorate are under real strain. Emergency department waiting times at Hillcrest Hospital have grown every year, and elective surgery lists are longer than they were three years ago.

If the government wants to talk about health, it should start by funding the hospital beds and nurses that patients are waiting for. Medicare must remain the foundation of the health system, and bulk billing rates for GP visits in regional areas deserve far more attention than they have received in this debate.

The economy has grown for twenty consecutive quarters and unemployment remains close to five per cent. Wages growth has been modest, and the government is aware that the cost of living is the first thing families raise with their members.

Building more homes is also an economic policy. Construction supports jobs for apprentices and small business, and investment in housing supply lifts productivity by letting workers live near where the jobs are.

The budget will return to surplus over the forward estimates without cutting the services Australians rely on. Interest rates are lower than when this government took office, which matters to every household with a mortgage.
